Quantum sensing is a technology that uses the rules of quantum physics to measure things much more precisely than traditional sensors.

The basic idea

Quantum sensing takes advantage of special quantum effects, such as:

Superposition – a quantum system can exist in multiple states at once

Entanglement – particles can be linked so that changes to one affect another

Quantum coherence – extremely stable, wave-like behavior at tiny scales

These effects make quantum systems extremely sensitive to tiny changes in their environment.

What can quantum sensors measure?

Quantum sensors can detect very small changes in:

Magnetic fields

Electric fields

Gravity

Time (atomic clocks)

Temperature

Motion and acceleration

Often, they can measure things that are too small for normal sensors to detect.

Examples of quantum sensing

Atomic clocks – use quantum transitions in atoms to keep incredibly accurate time (used in GPS)

Quantum magnetometers – detect tiny magnetic fields (used in brain scans and materials science)

Gravimeters – measure tiny variations in gravity (used for mapping underground structures)

NV-diamond sensors – use quantum states in diamonds to sense fields at the nanoscale

Why is it important?

Quantum sensing can:

Improve medical imaging (like better brain scans)

Help navigation without GPS

Detect underground resources or tunnels

Advance fundamental physics research

Improve precision in engineering and manufacturing

In simple terms

Quantum sensing uses quantum effects to build ultra-precise sensors that can detect extremely small changes in the world.
